skip_reason: Existing-move logistics / change-order call — not a sales call. Roselyn placed an outbound call to a customer who is already booked, opening with 'I'm actually just calling in we've got your email address. So I just wanted to ask some information with regards to your upcoming move.' Every topic is post-sale record maintenance on a job already on the schedule: correcting the mother's destination address ('16805 in Casana drive'), moving the date ('this is on October 6th instead of the 29th of September'), and scoping the additional stop at the brother's house that the customer had already flagged ('you did mention that we do have an additional stop'). No rate is quoted, no 'pricing is super simple' framing, no what's-included or no-hidden-fees pitch, no No Worries / Meet Your Mover / On-Time Guarantee, no clock explanation, no Save Your Ass prep speech, and no booking attempt — because the booking already exists. The only pricing-adjacent content is a re-estimate of the already-sold job to absorb the new stop ('we will be sending out still two vers and one truck estimated time that we have would be for six and a half hours... we have a drive time of thirty minutes and also we are getting or we have an additional stop'), which is estimate refinement on a booked move rather than an estimate presentation. This matches the established skip precedent for revised estimates on already-sold jobs (Chris Beattie 6582720638164992, Amy Arbasa 5029731778895872, Nicole Cruz 5993133672275968). Grading it against the 9-section sales scorecard would produce a misleadingly low number and pollute the run average.
top_strength: She scoped the added stop properly instead of just noting 'additional stop' and moving on. She got the item-level inventory ('what are we moving here? Are we moving the full house or like a specific item on?'), read it back to confirm ('the, that's dining table with chairs coo and the large chest for this one'), captured the floor count and staging ('And this is also a house? Is it a one story, a two story?' — customer: everything is in the garage or just inside the front door), asked about parking access at the second location, and pinned down the box count ('how many boxes are we're moving from this location?'). She also caught the drive-time impact herself ('this is like thirty minutes away from your location') and folded it into a revised 6.5-hour estimate rather than letting a new 30-minute leg silently blow the original quote. The reassurance on the estimate was the right instinct too: 'if they don't end up for 7:00 or 46 and a half then whatever the actual time is, that would only be the time that you need to pay, it's just that we need to make sure that the movers will be reserved for you on that day.' Both changes were closed with an email confirmation and an invitation to correct it ('I'll send you another email with regards to the second one and if ever that will be incorrect details just let me know as well').
coaching_note: Not graded — change-order call on an already-booked move. Three notes for the record if this call type ever gets its own rubric. First, the dead air. There are eight separate 'hold on / bear with me / give me one sec' stalls in a 6.7-minute call, several of them back to back ('Okay, give me one sec let me have this updated' → 'Okay. So this is, hold on, one check' → 'Okay? Give me one sec. I just need to have this updated'), so a large share of the call is the customer listening to her type. On a change order she should pull the record up before dialing and narrate while she works — 'While I get this updated, tell me what's coming out of your brother's garage' — instead of going silent. Second, the botched name in the opener: 'Hi good afternoon this is an from Einstein moving' — the rep's own name did not land. Third, and the only real accuracy risk: she never re-quoted the dollar figure after adding a 30-minute leg and a second load. The customer was told 6.5 hours and 'two vers and one truck' but never heard what that costs, so the line she needed was 'Manny, with your brother's stop added that puts you at about six and a half hours, which at your rate comes to roughly $X — the email I'm sending has the updated number at the top, so reply if anything looks off.' A scope change the customer approves without hearing the new total is the most common source of a move-day billing surprise.
phone_presence_notes: Polite and efficient with a warm close ('Alright then. Thank you so much. Have a great day') and a nice recovery when the customer admitted he had forgotten his brother's pickup ('Okay, no worries, bear with me'), but the call is largely transactional — the customer's name is never used once, there is no 'how are you today?', and long stretches are filled with 'hold on' while she works the record.
audio_review_reason: Transcript quality is poor in the spots that matter most: the rep's own name is garbled in the opener ('this is an from Einstein moving'), the estimate sentence is mangled ('if they don't end up for 7:00 or 46 and a half'), and inventory items come through as 'coo'/'curo'/'a curio a Alio' — so it cannot be confirmed from text alone whether she stated the hours and item list clearly to the customer.
